analysis.one_liner: Makes oil companies strictly liable for spills during ship-to-shore oil transfers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 1990 and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, where it died without a vote, a hearing, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make both the oil shipper and the shore facility jointly and strictly liable — meaning either one can be made to pay the whole bill — for cleanup costs and damages from oil spilled during a transfer between a tanker and an onshore facility. Covered damages include harm to natural resources, property, loss of subsistence use of those resources, and lost profits or earnings for people who depend on them. Defenses would be narrow: essentially acts of God, war, or a third party's sole fault.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents, fishermen, subsistence users of natural resources, businesses that depend on coastal property and resources, and taxpayers, who would no longer be left absorbing cleanup costs and damages from spills during oil transfers. Under the bill, claimants who derive at least a quarter of their earnings from activities using the damaged property or resources could recover lost profits or earnings, and any subsistence user could recover for lost subsistence use.

how_it_helps.text: Makes the vessel owner and the onshore facility owner jointly, severally, and strictly liable for removal costs and damages from oil spilled during transfers, so victims are not left arguing over which party was at fault.

Allows recovery for injury to natural resources, real or personal property, loss of subsistence use of natural resources, lost government revenues, and lost profits or earning capacity for people who derive at least 25 percent of their earnings from activities using the damaged property or resources.

Creates a rebuttable presumption that either the vessel or the facility party could have acted to prevent, minimize, or mitigate the discharge, making it harder for either side to shift blame onto the other.

analysis.who_pays: Oil shipping companies (vessel owners, operators, and charterers) and onshore oil terminal and facility owners, who would bear strict liability for the full cost of removal and damages from spills during transfers, including damages they might otherwise have avoided through fault-based legal fights.

drawbacks.text: Strict joint and several liability means one party can be forced to pay the entire cost of a spill even when the other party caused it, which industry could argue imposes costs disproportionate to any single company's role — though the bill does allow a defense when a third party's act or omission solely caused the incident.

The bill applies only to transfers between a vessel and an onshore facility, leaving spills from other causes outside its scope, and it contains no funding mechanism or liability limits beyond its defenses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who live and work near oil transfer points, the bill's benefit is straightforward: whoever spills oil during a ship-to-shore transfer — and their counterpart in the transfer — pays for the cleanup and the damages, rather than victims or taxpayers. The cost falls on oil shipping and terminal operators, who would face greater and less contestable financial exposure, a cost likely passed into oil transport prices. The strongest fair objection is that joint and several strict liability can make one party pay for another's fault, but the bill preserves defenses for acts of God, war, and third-party sole fault, and it was never debated, so no opposing case was ever put on the record.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in April 1990, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Bradley introduced the Oil Transfer Liability Act in the Senate on April 24, 1990.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, where no further action was taken.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil shipping and terminal operators, who avoided strict joint liability for spills during ship-to-shore transfers; coastal residents, fishermen, and taxpayers gained nothing, since the bill died without a vote.

for.name: Sen. Bill Bradley
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Oil Transfer Liability Act in the Senate on April 24, 1990.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.role: Senate committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on April 24, 1990, and never reported it, held no recorded action on it, and never allowed a floor vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote and drew no recorded opposition or support beyond its lone sponsor, so no partisan pattern appears in the record; it had zero cosponsors.

industries.note: Vessel owners, operators, and charterers would become strictly and jointly liable for the full cost of spills during transfers, including damages they could previously avoid by pointing at the other party. The bill died, so this exposure never materialized.

industries.industry: Onshore oil terminals and marine transfer facilities
industries.note: Facility owners and operators would share strict, joint liability with the vessel for transfer spills, covering removal costs plus natural resource, property, and lost-earnings damages. Because the bill died, they avoided this new liability entirely.

industries.industry: Commercial fishing, coastal tourism, and resource-dependent businesses
industries.note: The bill would let claimants who derive at least 25 percent of their earnings from activities using damaged property or natural resources recover lost profits or earning capacity, and subsistence users could recover for lost use. The industry's interest ran alongside the public's, but the bill's death left it without this new remedy.
